pos: n. (a widow’s life portion; a bride’s portion; a gift)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr., a gift; to give. Latin ]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines dower first as “That portion of the lands or tenements of a man which his widow enjoys during her life, after the death of her husband,” and notes, “This is the usual present signification of the word.” It also means “The property which a woman brings to her husband in marriage,” and “The gift of a husband for a wife.” For the third sense Webster cites Shechem’s offer: “Ask me never so much dowry and gift” (Gen 34:12). The law of Moses required the man who seduced a maid to “surely endow her to be his wife” (Exo 22:16). Dower in the first sense protects the widow, as Boaz raised up “the name of the dead upon his inheritance” (Rut 4:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DOWER, the portion of a man’s lands his widow enjoys for life; the property a woman brings in marriage; the gift of a husband for a wife; endowment.
webster_full: DOWER, noun [Gr., a gift; to give. Latin ]
1. That portion of the lands or tenements of a man which his widow enjoys during her life, after the death of her husband. [This is the usual present signification of the word.]
2. The property which a woman brings to her husband in marriage.
3. The gift of a husband for a wife.
Ask me never so much dowry and gift. Genesis 34:1.
4. Endowment; gift.
How great, how plentiful, how rich a dower
scriptures: Ask me never so much dowry and gift, and I will give according as ye shall say unto me: but give me the damsel to wife.
And if a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife.
Rut 4:10

Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day.
corruption_summary: Dower once secured a widow’s living from her husband’s land; the word records a law that put the widow first.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s chief sense is a widow’s life estate. The law made sure a husband’s death did not leave his wife destitute.
Scripture also guards the woman: a man who wrongs a maid must endow her (Exo 22:16).
roots_summary: Greek gift: the widow’s portion and the bride’s gift.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): that portion of the lands or tenements of a man which his widow enjoys during her life.
Webster: the gift of a husband for a wife.
Ask me never so much dowry and gift (Gen 34:12).
usage: The property which a woman brings to her husband in marriage

pos: n. (beating; a gun emplacement; in law, unlawful beating)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines battery first as “The act of battering, or beating.” In the military art it is “a parapet thrown up to cover the gunners,” with the guns employed. In law it is “the unlawful beating of another,” and he adds, “The least violence or the touching of another in anger is a battery.” God’s law made the striker answer for injury: if men strive and “one smite another with a stone, or with his fist,” the striker must “pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed” (Exo 21:18-19). Christ, struck unlawfully, asked, “If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?” (Joh 18:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BATTERY, the act of battering or beating; the instrument of battering; a parapet and guns in the military art; in law, the unlawful beating of another; an electrical or galvanic battery.
webster_full: BAT'TERY, noun [See Beat.]
1. The act of battering, or beating.
2. The instrument of battering.

3. In the military art, a parapet thrown up to cover the gunners and others employed about them, from the enemy's shot, with the guns employed. Thus, to erect a battery is to form the parapet and mount the guns. The term is applied also to a number of guns ranged in order for battering, and to mortars used for a like purpose.
Cross batteries are two batteries which play athwart each other, forming an angle upon the object battered.
Battery d'enfilade, is one which scours or sweeps the whole line or length.
Battery en echarpe, is that which plays obliquely.
Battery de revers, is that which plays upon the enemy's back.
Camerade battery is when several guns play at the same time upon one place.
4. In law, the unlawful beating of another. The least violence or the touching of another in anger is a battery

5. In electrical apparatus and experiments, a number of coated jars placed in such a manner, that they may be charged at the same time, and discharged in the same manner. This is called an electrical battery
6. Galvanic battery a pile or series of plates of copper and zink, or of any substances suspectable of galvanic action.
scriptures: And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed:
If he rise again, and walk abroad upon his staff, then shall he that smote him be quit: only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed.
Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?
Act 23:3
Then said Paul unto him, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?
corruption_summary: Webster’s legal battery begins with “the touching of another in anger”; the law protects the body God made.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster sets a low bar: “the least violence” in anger. The law treats the body of a neighbour as something not to be touched in wrath.
Paul protested being “smitten contrary to the law” (Act 23:3). Even a court may not strike unlawfully.
roots_summary: From beat: beating, and the guns that batter.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the act of battering, or beating.
Webster: in law, the unlawful beating of another.
Why smitest thou me? (Joh 18:23).

pos: n. (the crime of having two wives at once)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines bigamy as “The crime of having two wives at once,” and notes it “may be more justly defined, the crime of having a plurality of wives.” In canon law it was “the marrying a second wife after the death of the first, or once marrying a widow,” which “disqualified a man for orders.” Scripture’s pattern from creation is one man and one wife: “they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24). Christ restated it: “they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5). An elder must be “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BIGAMY, the crime of having two wives at once, ordinarily synonymous with polygamy; in canon law, marrying a second wife after the first’s death, or marrying a widow.
webster_full: BIG'AMY, noun [Latin bis, twice]
The crime of having two wives at once. But the term is ordinarily used as synonymous with Polygamy, and may be more justly defined, the crime of having a plurality of wives.
In the canon law, bigamy was the marrying a second wife after the death of the first, or once marrying a widow. This disqualified a man for orders, and holding ecclesiastical offices.
scriptures: Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Mat 19:5
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
corruption_summary: Webster calls bigamy a crime; Scripture calls marriage “one flesh,” which leaves no room for a second wife.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s first word is “crime.” A marriage law that protects the one-flesh union protects wives and children.
Webster records that the canon-law sense “disqualified a man for orders.” Scripture’s own rule for elders is “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2).
roots_summary: Latin bis, twice: two wives at once.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the crime of having two wives at once.
Webster: the crime of having a plurality of wives.
They shall be one flesh (Gen 2:24).
usage: The crime of having two wives at once

pos: n. (the losing of a right or estate by an offense)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines forfeiture as “The act of forfeiting; the losing of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition or other act.” He adds that “In regard to property, forfeiture is a loss of the right to possess, but not generally the actual possession, which is to be transferred by some subsequent process.” Ezra’s order used the penalty: whoever would not come “all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation” (Ezr 10:8). Scripture also shows forfeiture abused. After Naboth’s judicial murder, Jezebel told Ahab, “Arise, take possession of the vineyard” (1Ki 21:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORFEITURE, the losing of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office or effects by an offense, crime, or breach of condition; that which is forfeited; a fine.
webster_full: FOR'FEITURE, noun

1. The act of forfeiting; the losing of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition or other act. In regard to property, forfeiture is a loss of the right to possess, but not generally the actual possession, which is to be transferred by some subsequent process. In the feudal system, a forfeiture of lands gave him in reversion or remainder a right to enter.
2. That which is forfeited; an estate forfeited; a fine or mulet. The prince enriched his treasury by fines and forfeitures.
scriptures: Ezr 10:8

And that whosoever would not come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away.

And it came to pass, when Jezebel heard that Naboth was stoned, and was dead, that Jezebel said to Ahab, Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give thee for money: for Naboth is not alive, but dead.

Notwithstanding no devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the LORD of all that he hath, both of man and beast, and of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: Forfeiture is a lawful penalty for an offense proved; seizure without a true offense is Ahab’s sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster ties forfeiture to “an offense, crime, breach of condition.” Without a real offense there is no forfeiture, only theft by law.
Naboth’s vineyard was taken through false witnesses (1Ki 21:15). Process does not make a taking just.
roots_summary: From forfeit: a right lost by an offense.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the act of forfeiting.
Webster: that which is forfeited; an estate forfeited.
All his substance should be forfeited (Ezr 10:8).
usage: By an offense, crime, breach of condition

pos: n. & v. (an estate limited in descent; to settle descent; to fix on descendants)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines an entail as “An estate or fee entailed,” and also as a “Rule of descent settled for an estate.” The verb is “To settle the descent of lands and tenements, by gift to a man and to certain heirs specified, so that neither the donee nor any subsequent possessor can alienate or bequeath it.” Its figurative sense is “To fix unalienably on a person or thing, or on a person and his descendants,” as in his examples: “By the apostasy misery is supposed to be entailed on mankind,” and “The intemperate often entail infirmities, diseases and ruin on their children.” Israel’s land worked like an entail: “every one of the children of Israel shall keep himself to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers” (Num 36:7). Sin is entailed too: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Rom 5:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENTAIL, an estate limited in descent to particular heirs; a rule of descent; v. to settle the descent of lands so that no possessor can alienate it; to fix unalienably on a person and his descendants.
webster_full: ENTA'IL, noun
1. An estate or fee entailed,

Estates-tail are general, as when lands and tenements are given to one and the heirs of his body begotten; or special, as when lands and tenements are given to one and the heirs of his body by a particular wife.
2. Rule of descent settled for an estate.
3. Engraver's work; inlay.

ENTA'IL, verb transitive To settle the descent of lands and tenements, by gift to a man and to certain heirs specified, so that neither the donee nor any subsequent possessor can alienate or bequeath it; as, to entail a manor to AB and to his eldest son, or to his heirs of his body begotten, or to his heirs by a particular wife.

1. To fix unalienably on a person or thing, or on a person and his descendants. By the apostasy misery is supposed to be entailed on mankind. The intemperate often entail infirmities, diseases and ruin on their children.
scriptures: Num 36:7
So shall not the inheritance of the children of Israel remove from tribe to tribe: for every one of the children of Israel shall keep himself to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.
A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
corruption_summary: Entail is a legal word for what a father passes to his children; Webster says it can be land, or ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s examples are moral: misery entailed by the apostasy, ruin entailed by intemperance. A man’s habits fall on his children.
The better entail is the one Proverbs commends: “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children” (Pro 13:22).
roots_summary: Lands fixed in descent, and what a man fixes on his heirs.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): rule of descent settled for an estate.
Webster: to fix unalienably on a person or thing, or on a person and his descendants.
Every one ... shall keep himself to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers (Num 36:7).
usage: By the apostasy misery is supposed to be entailed on mankind

pos: n. (the killing of a human being by another; a manslayer)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin homicidium; homo, man, and caedo, to strike, to kill.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines homicide as “The killing of one man or human being by another,” and divides it into three kinds: “justifiable, excusable, and felonious.” It is excusable “when it happens from misadventure, or in self-defense,” and felonious “when it proceeds from malice.” “homicide committed with premeditated malice, is murder.” Scripture draws the same lines. The ground of the law is the image of God: “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Gen 9:6). For the man who killed without lying in wait, God appointed “a place whither he shall flee” (Exo 21:13), the cities of refuge for one who “killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): HOMICIDE, the killing of one human being by another, justifiable, excusable or felonious; with premeditated malice it is murder; also a manslayer.
webster_full: HOM'ICIDE, noun [Latin homicidium; homo, man, and caedo, to strike, to kill.]

1. The killing of one man or human being by another. homicide is of three kinds, justifiable, excusable, and felonious; justifiable, when it proceeds from unavoidable necessity, without an intention to kill, and without negligence; excusable, when it happens from misadventure, or in self-defense; felonious, when it proceeds from malice, or is done in the prosecution of some unlawful act, or in a sudden passion. homicide committed with premeditated malice, is murder. Suicide also, or self-murder, is felonious homicide homicide comprehends murder and manslaughter.
1. A person who kills another; a manslayer.
scriptures: Gen 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee.
Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
corruption_summary: Homicide is a broad word; the law and Scripture both distinguish murder from killing by accident.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s three kinds of homicide follow the shape of Mosaic law: malice, misadventure, necessity. The intent of the heart matters.
The cities of refuge protected the accidental slayer from the avenger (Num 35:11). Justice weighs the act and the heart behind it.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the killing of one man or human being by another.
Webster: homicide committed with premeditated malice, is murder.
In the image of God made he man (Gen 9:6).
usage: A person who kills another; a manslayer

pos: n. (a laying down; sworn written testimony; removal from office)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines deposition as “The act of laying or throwing down,” and in law as “The act of giving testimony under oath” and “The attested written testimony of a witness; an affidavit.” A further sense is “The act of dethroning a king, or the degrading of a person from an office or station.” Webster adds that “A deposition differs from abdication; an abdication being voluntary, and a deposition compulsory.” God’s law tests testimony: “the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness” (Deu 19:18). God deposes proud rulers: Nebuchadnezzar “was deposed from his kingly throne” (Dan 5:20). “He hath put down the mighty from their seats” (Luk 1:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEPOSITION, the act of laying down; that which is lodged; the act of giving testimony under oath; attested written testimony; the dethroning of a king or degrading from office.
webster_full: DEPOSITION, noun
1. The act of laying or throwing down; as, soil is formed by the deposition of fine particles, during a flood.
2. That which is thrown down; that which is lodged; as, banks are sometimes depositions of alluvial matter.
3. The act of giving testimony under oath.
4. The attested written testimony of a witness; an affidavit.

5. The act of dethroning a king, or the degrading of a person from an office or station; a divesting of sovereignty, or of office and dignity; a depriving of clerical orders. A deposition differs from abdication; an abdication being voluntary, and a deposition compulsory.
scriptures: And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
Dan 5:20
But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:
Luk 1:52
He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
corruption_summary: A deposition is sworn testimony or a ruler’s removal; in both, truth and God’s judgment stand behind the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster lists sworn testimony beside the dethroning of kings. A witness and a king both answer to a higher authority.
Pride brought Nebuchadnezzar down (Dan 5:20). No throne is safe from the God who “hath put down the mighty” (Luk 1:52).
roots_summary: A laying down: of testimony under oath, or of a ruler from his seat.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the act of giving testimony under oath.
Webster: the act of dethroning a king.
He was deposed from his kingly throne (Dan 5:20).
usage: The attested written testimony of a witness; an affidavit
An abdication being voluntary, and a deposition compulsory
